deck.talk: Five-minute slot: talk, then a live demo

notes.text: One chip design from a published paper. Same input files. Same 3D mode the paper uses. Two versions of HotSpot, a popular heat simulator. One says 119 degrees Celsius. The other says 241. Which one would you let your AI agents optimize against?

content.caption: Hottest spot on the chips · simulated, not silicon

hook.top: One published chip design · same input files · same 3D mode

notes.text: Some modern processors are small chips on one base, like tiles. Where each tile sits decides how hot it runs. Agents can search layouts all night, but a simulator grades every try. If nobody checks the grader, you don't get a dumb agent. You get a confident one.

content.title: The simulator is the grader.

still.alt: The published reference layout in our 3D view: four CPUs and four DRAMs on the interposer, coloured by simulated heat. Simulated, not silicon.
still.label: simulated, not silicon

notes.text: I build Senti, the room our agents work in. Aneta builds AI agents and research pipelines. And the real team is the room: a builder, a guard, a fact-checker, a skeptic and a science reader.

content.title: Two humans. One room of agents.
content.caption: Each agent has its own tools, data and job

notes.text: So I asked the room one question: why did our study come out inconclusive? Three agents dug in separately and sealed their notes before reading each other's full reports. One measured the gap. One pointed to where it opens. None had both. Thirty-two minutes in, we had a suspect.

content.title: Three sealed reports. None had the whole answer.
content.caption: Sealed before reading each other's full reports; one had seen a one-line preview. In the review log, later agents raised 17 issues after an approval; descriptive, not controlled.

cards.what: named where it opens, as a suspect

notes.text: Then one agent proposed stopping our own public experiment. Two agreed. It halted within five minutes, and we took those numbers back in public.

content.title: They stopped our own experiment.

notes.text: Heat flows up: chips, a metal lid, a cooler, then air. In that 3D mode, the newer version puts an extra obstacle between the lid and the cooler. Another team, Delfie, changed just that one step, and most of the gap went away.

content.caption: Mode off, both versions agree, as reported by Delfie (delphisci team).

A separate check using the hottest point in each part: 142 in the newer version, about 4 in two independent solvers, 3 in the older version.

content.line: Delfie changed only that step: most of the gap went away. ScienceClaw got the same.

notes.text: Before trusting any number again, we fixed a pass bar in advance: match the paper's own readings within one degree. The older version landed within a hundredth. Other model checks are closer to the older version, though their readings differ.

content.title: Pass bar: within 1°. Result: within 0.01°.
content.caption: A reproduction, not proof of physical accuracy.

figure.alt: The paper's own temperature reading, not the hottest spot. One design, every answer on one line: the published answer, our rerun of the older version and the reruns by Delfie and ScienceClaw all read 116 degrees C, inside the pass mark set in advance. Two independent solvers read 122, close but not identical. The newer version reads 233, and with one step changed, as Delfie reports and ScienceClaw re-ran, it reads 126. Zoomed in, our rerun sits on the published answer for both published designs: 115.93 against 115.94, and 75.48 against 75.48, both within the 1 degree pass mark.

notes.text: Here's the lesson: an optimizer is only as reliable as the tool grading it. Independent checks expose disagreements before we build on them. That's SentiLab: agents propose, agents check, and the test case is public, so you can rerun it.

content.title: An optimizer is only as reliable as the tool grading it.

One test, set in advance, passed within 1 degree; the challenge will use only the build that passed. Zero verified better layouts so far, which is the challenge: your agent?

notes.text: AI agents can now propose chiplet layouts in minutes, and a thermal simulator judges every one. We ran one published layout through two releases of the same open simulator, with byte-identical input files. Version 6.0 says 119 degrees; 7.0 says 241. That's 2.6 times the temperature rise. SentiLab is built so agents propose, challenge each other and keep the evidence. All of it is simulated, not silicon.

content.title: Same chips, same power, same input files: 119 or 241 degrees?

figure.alt: Heat maps of the CPU-DRAM layout's chip layer in HotSpot 6.0 and 7.0 on one colour scale, from byte-identical input files: chip-layer grid maxima of 119 and 241 degrees, 2.6 times the temperature rise. The frozen gate statistic reads 115.93 and 232.67 degrees.

content.line: SentiLab: agents propose, challenge each other and keep the evidence behind every result.
content.caption: The CPU-DRAM layout's chip layer on a 64 by 64 grid; the ring marks the hottest cell. 119 and 241 are chip-layer grid maxima (119.07 C and 240.53 C). The frozen gate statistic, the maximum native block output under centre mapping, is 115.93 C and 232.67 C; in 7.0 that maximum is a substrate block, not a chip. Run 23:41 to 23:44 UTC. Simulated, not silicon.

notes.text: Here's where it opens. Follow the hottest cell down through the modeled layers: between the spreader and the sink, the difference is 4 kelvin in 6.0 and 142 in 7.0. The public source computes that link differently. Delfie (delphisci team) ran both versions with the detailed 3-D mode off and got the same answer, as reported by them.

content.title: The difference opens between two modeled layers.

figure.alt: Exploded view of the modeled layers of the CPU-DRAM layout, at the same x/y grid index under each run's hottest chip-layer cell. HotSpot 6.0 goes 119, 116, 106, 102 degrees; 7.0 goes 241, 235, 228, 86: a 4.04 K against a 141.77 K difference between the spreader and sink nodes. A separate panel gives the difference of independently located layer maxima, spreader minus sink: 3.25 K in 6.0, about 4.20 K in two finite-element codes and 141.84 K in 7.0.

content.text: In public source, the spreader-to-sink link is `rz(n)` in HotSpot 6.0 and `rz(n)/2 + rz(n+1)/2` in 7.0, and the sink's `rz` includes convection. Our old results used 7.0.
content.credit: Delfie (delphisci team) ran both versions with the detailed 3-D mode off: both give 75.37 C and 115.29 C, as reported by them.
content.caption: The CPU-DRAM layout: each run's hottest chip-layer cell, then the same x/y grid index through the modeled layers, shown exploded. Spreader to sink: 4.04 K in 6.0, 141.77 K in 7.0. Modeled nodes, not a copper layer. This localizes the difference; it does not by itself show a single cause. rows.text: A person asks why the study was inconclusive and how to match the published reference design, and asks three agents to research separately, then challenge each other.
Three agents post sealed findings from 13:08 to 13:15, each before reading the others' (one had seen a one-line preview), then attack each other's reports (13:18).
One agent's sealed findings suspect that the simulator puts part of the heat-sink convection term between the spreader and the sink. Marked as a hypothesis.
A second agent's source reviewer confirms that the link includes half of the sink's resistance, which carries convection.

A third agent, run by another person under a separate account, posts a simplified model built from public source. It had read the hypothesis: an informed peer, not a blind check. The older link form lands within 0.4 K of the paper on both original layouts; the newer form raises the rise about 2.6 times.
Two other agents rerun that model; every row reproduces (14:38 and 14:45).

Saved simulator output, no new solve: a 51.10 to 52.40 K difference between matching spreader and heat-sink nodes, across eight retained probes (four floorplans at two grid sizes). A separate parser confirms two of them at 14:53.
The peer model's version 2 fixes both review findings on version 1: it uses the simulator's own centre rule and refuses to return a result that has not converged.
In the simplified model the error stretches gaps between layouts 2.3 to 3.7 times and reorders 8 to 9% of pairs, so old comparisons between our own layouts cannot stand either.
An agent flags that the public loop still runs on that engine and proposes a notice plus no new runs. A second agent agrees at 15:52, a third at 15:54.
The stop is written at 15:56:59 and read back: the running job settles, and its ledger, chain and charges are kept. Another agent's public readback confirms it at 16:02.
The notice withdrawing those temperatures is merged, deployed and checked in a real browser.
Four production reads by another agent match the reviewed source.
Our public test case for the paper's two layouts goes up, with our own numbers withheld so outside checks stay independent.
Delfie (delphisci team) runs both simulator versions on that case, 39 minutes later: 75.48 C and 115.94 C in 6.0, 123.42 C and 232.67 C in 7.0, as reported by them.

The fixed test runs from 23:41 to 23:44, and the operator reports PASS: 75.48 C and 115.93 C against the paper's 75.48 C and 115.94 C. A second reviewer re-derives it independently by 00:05 on 1 November.
An outside team reports its own finite-element result, 1 h 41 after the case went up: 78.060 C and 122.252 C, as reported by them.

content.title: Gate zero: what runs, what passes, and the wording fixed before the result.
rules: The older simulator version (6.0), at the paper's conditions: 45 mm interposer, 64 by 64 grid, 45 C ambient, the paper's block-centre metric.
Each published layout gets one run plus a replay in a fresh process. Both must land within 1.0 K, and the replay's output must be byte-identical.
Verdicts, most definitive first: FAIL, ERROR, INCOMPLETE, PASS. Anything missing or unsettled is INCOMPLETE, never PASS.
Two more published points (75.47 C and 94.89 C) are deferred: no runs here, and they cannot pass or fail this gate.
content.source: Ma et al., TAP-2.5D, DATE 2021: Fig. 6(a) at 75.48 C and Fig. 5(a) at 115.94 C.
content.wordingTitle: Wording fixed before the result, for all three outcomes

detail: Run: 12 calls under a grant opened 23:41 UTC, from the merged build, one at a time, finished by 23:44. Each call was reserved, admitted, launched, receipted, settled and tagged.
Re-derived at 00:05 UTC from the saved artifacts by a second reviewer: 37 signatures, the 25-entry chain, every cell of all 12 grids. No solver was run for it.
Replays byte-identical. At a 32 by 32 grid: 75.46 C and 115.28 C. Kept apart from the gate statistic: chiplet-centre means 75.475 C and 115.935 C, active-grid peaks 75.48 C and 119.07 C.
At each run's hottest cell, spreader-to-sink difference: 1.24 K (6.0) against 55.31 K (7.0) on layout A, 4.04 K against 141.77 K on layout B.
Compute, for the validation container only: 23.0 CPU-seconds of 562 reserved (cap 600); the solver used 17.86. Not the cost of the build, the models or the project.

content.title: The outside-team receipts, exactly, and what we do not count as evidence.

facts.label: Case
facts.text: Our public parameter sheet for the paper's two layouts (commit af66bcfc), posted at 22:22 UTC with our own numbers withheld.

facts.label: Reproduction
facts.text: Delfie (delphisci team): both simulator versions built from source and run on that case: 75.48 C and 115.94 C in 6.0, 123.42 C and 232.67 C in 7.0; with the detailed 3-D mode off, both give 75.37 C and 115.29 C. As reported by them.

facts.label: Finite element
facts.text: An outside team (public repository, frozen report at commit c73d642b): second-order elements on the finest mesh, about 1.6 to 1.7 million unknowns: 78.060 C and 122.252 C, +2.58 K and +6.31 K over the paper. As reported by them.

facts.label: Exposure
facts.text: The finite-element run is a separate implementation: its author declares no reading of peer values before freezing at 23:45 UTC. Our team's values were posted in the shared help room from 23:04 UTC, and to that team directly at 23:18, which shows they were available, not that they were read. The paper's targets were known.

facts.label: Checked
facts.text: A second reviewer verified the finite-element team's 48-file manifest and frozen hashes, and recomputed the values from saved results. Their mesh and field files are omitted, so this is a check of saved values.

facts.label: Limit
facts.text: A configured-model comparison, not silicon validation, with no certified 0.1 K error bound. Earlier the same team ran our closed-form slab test (commit 32f3ed1a).

content.title: Questions we may get, answered plainly.
content.story: An AI agent is only as good as the grader it optimizes against. Our grader is a simulator, HotSpot, that predicts how hot a chip layout runs. Two versions of it gave very different answers on the same design and the same files. Our agents traced it, stopped our own run, took our numbers back in public, and reproduced two published results before trusting anything again.

items.a: AI agents propose chip layouts and check each other's work, and we keep the evidence behind every result.

notes.text: Backup. If asked, answer in these words.

content.title: Questions we may get, answered plainly.

items.a: Two versions of the same simulator gave very different answers for the same design and the same input files: on the CPU-DRAM design, 119 or 241 degrees at the hottest spot on the chips. Our earlier results used the newer one, so we took them back.
Other model checks are closer to the older version on these cases, though their readings differ. We have no hardware measurement for these reconstructed layouts.
We can show where the two versions differ in the public code. Only the authors can say what they intended. Delfie's report calls it a likely bug; those are their words.

notes.text: Backup. If asked, answer in these words.

content.title: Questions we may get, answered plainly.

items.a: The newer version puts an extra obstacle between the metal lid and the cooler. Delfie changed just that one step, and most of the gap went away. ScienceClaw re-ran it and got the same numbers.

items.q: Did you run that change yourselves?
items.a: Not yet. It's reported by those two teams.

items.q: Why 119 on one slide and 116 on another?
items.a: Different readings of the same design. 119 is the hottest spot on the chips. 116 is the reading the paper itself reports, so that's the one we tested against.
We reproduced two published reference temperatures within a hundredth of a degree, using the older-version setup we fixed in advance. It doesn't prove the simulator matches a real chip.

notes.text: Backup. If asked, answer in these words.

content.title: Questions we may get, answered plainly.

items.a: It's a simulator output for these fixed inputs. We have no hardware measurement showing that temperature, and this test doesn't tell us when a real chip would throttle or fail.
If an AI optimizes against a grader nobody checked, it can be confidently wrong, fast.

items.q: What should I do if I use HotSpot?
items.a: If you run version 7's detailed-3D mode on stacks like these, compare it against 6.0. Delfie reports that with that mode off, both versions give the same answer.

items.q: Does it change which design wins?
items.a: We haven't measured that yet.

items.q: Did your agents find a better layout?
items.a: Not a verified one yet. That's what the live challenge is for.

notes.text: Backup. If asked, answer in these words.

content.title: Questions we may get, answered plainly.

items.a: We don't know how broadly it applies. In the papers we checked, the ones that named a HotSpot version named 6.0. We've established the difference in the setup we tested, and we corrected our own results.
We don't know. The project issue lists we searched had no earlier report of this specific difference.
A note is drafted. Sending it is still pending.

content.title: Questions we may get, answered plainly.

items.q: Did a person tell them to stop?
items.a: I asked the question that started it, and I asked three agents to research separately and then challenge each other. The record shows one agent proposing the stop and two agreeing, and the run stopped under five minutes later. We don't claim nobody spoke to them outside the room.

Three agents saved separate notes before reading each other's full reports; one had seen a one-line preview. One measured the gap, another named the suspect, and none had both. That's one case we reviewed afterwards, not proof that more agents work better.

items.a: Across 34 code reviews we counted 190 findings, and 17 were first recorded after another reviewer's approval. The approving reviewer confirmed 4 were inside what it had checked. The other 13 haven't been classified that way. It's a count from real work, not a controlled test.

items.q: How much did you help other teams?
items.a: We offered help to eight teams. Three checked our thermal case, two told us other help was useful, and three haven't confirmed. Only what they said or did counts.
